title: Flesh (sarx)
lead: The Greek word sarx, 'flesh', means the soft body of a person or animal and, by extension, a human being in his weakness; in Paul it can also name human life in its fallen state, set against God's Spirit. English versions that translate it 'sinful nature' choose one reading among several. This site keeps 'flesh' and explains the sense at each place.

sections.b: Paul uses sarx for (1) the physical body ('the life I now live in the flesh', Galatians 2:20); (2) human descent ('Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh', Romans 4:1; the Israelites 'according to the flesh', Romans 9:3); (3) humanity as weak and mortal ('no flesh will be justified', Galatians 2:16); and (4) humanity under the power of sin, opposed to the Spirit ('the flesh desires what is against the Spirit', Galatians 5:17). Readers argue whether (4) names a part of the person or an age and power; the Greek allows both.
